title: Answer every interested reply within the hour
summary: Find replies that show interest, draft an answer that books the call, and send it once you approve.
description: An interested reply goes cold fast. Answering within the hour books far more meetings than answering the next day, but replies land across many mailboxes and sequencers. This playbook reads the inbox, picks out the replies that ask a question or show interest, drafts a short answer that moves to a meeting, and waits for you to approve each one.

connections.label: An AI model, unless you run this from your own AI app

steps.say: List replies from the last day that nobody has answered yet.
Read each conversation and keep the ones that are interested or ask a question.
Tag them so the team sees them.
Draft a short reply in the same thread that answers the question and offers the booking link.

guardrails: Every reply waits for a person to approve it before it is sent.
Out-of-office, unsubscribe and not-interested replies are left alone.

measure.how: Median minutes from an interested reply to our answer.
Share of interested replies that become a booked meeting.

prompt: Run the "Answer interested replies" playbook. Go through replies from the last 24 hours that nobody has answered. Keep the ones that show interest or ask a question, and tag them "Interested". For each one, draft a short, friendly answer in the same thread that answers their question and offers a time to talk with {{booking_link}}. Leave out-of-office, unsubscribe and not-interested replies alone. Hold every reply for my approval.
example: Of 140 replies one morning, 9 were interested. Each got a three-line answer drafted with the booking link; the team approved them in a few minutes and 4 booked a call the same day.

title: Fix your SEO quick wins
summary: Crawl your site, find the issues that cost the most clicks, and turn each one into a fix your team or coding agent can ship.
description: Most sites have a handful of problems that cost far more than the rest: pages that rank on page two for searches with real volume, broken pages that still get links, missing titles on pages people do find. This playbook crawls the site, reads Search Console, and ranks the fixes by the clicks they are likely to bring.

steps.say: Find the site and crawl it.
Read what the audit found and how the site does in search.
Rank the fixes by the clicks they are likely to bring and keep the top ten.
Turn each one into a prompt a coding agent can work from.

guardrails: Never changes the site itself; fixes go to the fixes list for a person or a coding agent.

measure.how: Search Console clicks to the fixed pages, 28 days before and after.

prompt: Run the "SEO quick wins" playbook for {{site}}. Crawl the site, read what the audit found and how its pages do in Google Search Console, and rank the problems by how many clicks fixing them is likely to bring. Give me the top ten as fixes, each with a prompt I can hand to a coding agent.
example: For northpeak.example the top fix was a pricing page ranking 11th for a search with 2,400 monthly impressions and no meta description; the second was a broken docs page that still had 14 links pointing at it.

title: Tag every link you share
summary: Find the traffic you can't credit to a channel and give every link you share a campaign tag.
description: When links go out without tags, visits and sign-ups land in "direct" or "unknown" and nobody can tell which channel worked. This playbook looks at where your site's visits come from, finds the channels with untagged traffic, and makes tagged campaign links for each one, using one spelling for every source.

connections.label: Your web analytics, to compare with what Outflare sees

steps.say: Read the channels and sources campaign links can use.
Compare where visits come from with the campaigns that exist, and list the channels with untagged traffic.
Create a campaign for each gap and a tagged link for every place the brand shares links.

guardrails: Only creates campaigns and links; it never changes your site or posts anything.

measure.how: Share of visits with a known channel and campaign, before and after.

prompt: Run the "Tag every link" playbook for {{brand}}. Look at where the site's visits come from and which campaigns already exist, and tell me which channels send traffic we can't credit. Then create a campaign for each gap and a tagged link for every place we share links (newsletter, social profiles, partner pages, email signatures), and give me the list.
example: Northpeak found that 31% of sign-ups came from "unknown". Most were from the newsletter and two partner blogs; three campaigns and eight links fixed it the same week.

title: Welcome new sign-ups and get them to their first win
summary: A short welcome journey that follows what each new user does, not how many days have passed.
description: Most welcome emails go out on a timer: day 1, day 3, day 7. People who already got going get told how to start, and people who are stuck get nothing useful. This playbook finds the one action that tells you a new user got value (their first API call, first project, first purchase), then builds a journey that stops as soon as they take it and nudges them with a specific next step until they do.

data.label: Sign-up and product events sent to Outflare

connections.label: An email provider for lifecycle email
An AI model, unless you run this from your own AI app

inputs.name: first_win
inputs.label: What a first win looks like
inputs.help: The action that shows a new user got value. Leave it empty and the agent suggests one from your events.

steps.say: Read the brand's context so the emails sound like the brand.
Look at the events new users send in their first week and pick the one that best marks a first win, unless one was given.
Write three short emails (welcome, a nudge with one concrete next step, and a last helpful tip) as templates.
Build a journey that starts on sign-up, sends the emails, and exits as soon as the first-win event arrives.
Ask a person to turn the journey on.

guardrails: Only people who signed up themselves get these emails, and the contact rules and opt-outs apply to every send.
The journey is turned on only after a person approves it.

measure.how: Share of new sign-ups who reach the first win within 7 days, before and after.
Median hours from sign-up to the first-win event.

prompt: Run the "Welcome new sign-ups" playbook for {{brand}}. Look at the events new users send in their first week and find the action that best shows they got value (use "{{first_win}}" if I gave one). Then write three short, plain emails in our voice: a welcome, a nudge with one concrete next step, and a final tip. Build a lifecycle journey that starts on sign-up, sends them over the first week, and stops as soon as someone reaches that first win. Don't turn the journey on: show me the emails and the journey first.
example: Northpeak's events showed that users who create a project in their first day stay three times longer. The journey sends a welcome straight away, "Create your first project in two minutes" after a day, and a template gallery link after three days, and leaves anyone who already created one.

title: Find creators who already cover your competitors
summary: Videos, newsletters and podcasts that reviewed or sponsored a competitor, vetted and pitched, all tracked on your Partnerships board.
description: A creator who reviewed a competitor has shown three things: their audience cares about your category, they take sponsorships, and they can explain a product like yours. This playbook finds who covered your competitors in the last year, drops the ones that are off-topic or too small, and drafts a personal pitch for each one you approve, with a partnership on the board for every creator so nothing gets lost.

data.label: A mailbox to send pitches from

connections.label: Web search, unless your AI app searches the web itself
Social search, to find posts that mention your competitors
An AI model, unless you run this from your own AI app

inputs.name: competitors
inputs.label: Competitors
inputs.help: Two to five names, the way people write them.

inputs.name: platforms
inputs.label: Where to look
inputs.help: Leave it empty to look everywhere your buyers might be.

steps.say: Read the brand's context, and check its setup kit is applied so the Partnerships board and creator fields are there.
Look at partnerships already on the board, so nobody is pitched twice.
Find reviews, comparisons and sponsored posts about each competitor from the last twelve months, with the brand's social watches and web search.
For each creator behind them, find or add a person with their platforms, audience size, topics and past sponsors, and a partnership at Found.
Vet each one (topic fit, recent views, how the review read) and move them to Vetted or Declined with a one-line reason.
Draft a short pitch for each vetted creator that names what they said about the competitor and why your product is worth a look, as a sequence held until a person approves the sends.
Move partnerships to Pitched when the sequence runs, and to Negotiating or Declined as replies come in.

guardrails: Never send a pitch, accept terms or promise money without a person's approval.
Never criticise a competitor in a pitch; say what your product does better.
Only use contact details a creator publishes for business, and never contact anyone who opted out.

measure.how: Replies from pitched creators divided by creators pitched.
Partnerships that reach Agreed within 30 days.

prompt: Find creators who already cover {{brand}}'s competitors: {{competitors}}. Look at {{platforms}} for reviews, comparisons and sponsored posts from the last year. Vet them, put each one on the Partnerships board, and draft a personal pitch for the best ten. Nothing is sent until I approve it.
example: Northpeak named two competitors. The agent found 64 videos and 18 newsletters that reviewed them, kept 22 that were on-topic with at least 2,000 views, and drafted 12 pitches. Four replied and two agreed: a newsletter slot for 400 USD and a video for 900 USD.

title: Get named in AI answers
summary: See which questions AI assistants answer without naming you, and what to publish so they do.
description: People ask ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity which tool to use. If the answer names three competitors and not you, you lose the sale before anyone visits your site. This playbook samples the questions buyers ask in your category, finds the ones where competitors are named and you aren't, reads the pages the assistants cite, and lists what to publish or correct.

connections.label: An AI model to ask the questions

inputs.name: category
inputs.label: What you sell, in a few words
inputs.example: project planning software for small agencies

steps.say: Read how often AI answers name the brand today.
Add a set of buyer questions for the category if there isn't one.
Read the answers where competitors are named and the brand isn't, and the pages they cite.
Compare with what competitors publish.
Post a short list of pages to write or facts to correct.

guardrails: Questions are asked with the workspace's own AI key, within its monthly AI limit.

measure.how: Share of sampled answers that name the brand, before and after.

prompt: Run the "Get named in AI answers" playbook for {{brand}}, which sells {{category}}. Check how often AI assistants name us today. If there's no set of buyer questions for our category, add one. Then find the answers that name competitors but not us, read the pages they cite, and give me a short list of pages to write or facts to correct so we get named.
example: Northpeak was named in 4 of 40 answers about agency project tools. Most answers cited two comparison pages and a review site, none of which listed Northpeak; the list started with asking those three to add it.

title: Recruit affiliates and creators from your own sign-ups
summary: Find the people who signed up and run a blog, channel, newsletter or comparison site in your space, and invite them to partner with you.
description: Some of your best partners already use your product. A sign-up from a company whose website is a review site, a developer blog or a YouTube channel about your category can send you customers who trust them. This playbook reads recent sign-ups, looks at the website behind each one, picks those with a real audience in your topic, puts them on the Partnerships board, and drafts a personal invite for each one you approve: a commission on every sale, free product, or a paid post.

data.label: People who signed up, with their company or website

connections.label: An email provider for invites to your own users
A way to read their websites, unless your AI app can
An AI model, unless you run this from your own AI app

inputs.name: topics
inputs.label: Your space
inputs.help: What a partner's audience should care about.

inputs.name: offer
inputs.label: What you offer partners
inputs.help: Leave it empty and the agent suggests a commission, free product or a paid post for each one.

steps.say: Read the brand's context, and check its setup kit is applied so the Partnerships board is there.
List people who signed up in the period, with their companies and websites, and skip anyone already on the board or who opted out of marketing email.
Look at the website behind each one and note what it is (review or comparison site, blog, newsletter, channel, agency, or a normal business), its topics and any sign of an audience.
For each one with an audience in the space, save their creator fields and add a partnership at Found with a suggested deal type, and a one-line reason.
Draft a short, personal invite for each, from a real person at the brand, that says why them and what they'd get. Hold every send until a person approves it.
Move partnerships to Pitched when the invite goes out, and to Negotiating or Declined as replies come in.

guardrails: Never send an invite or agree terms without a person's approval.
Only write to people who allow marketing email from the brand; the opt-out list always wins.
Never mention what you know about their account or usage beyond the fact that they signed up.

measure.how: Sign-ups added to the board divided by sign-ups reviewed.
Partnerships from this playbook that reach Agreed within 30 days.

prompt: Find partners among {{brand}}'s own sign-ups from {{since}}. Look at the website behind each one and pick the people who run a blog, channel, newsletter or comparison site about {{topics}}. Put them on the Partnerships board and draft a personal invite for each, offering {{offer}}. Nothing is sent until I approve it.
example: Northpeak reviewed 1,240 sign-ups from the last 90 days. 31 came from websites with an audience: 12 running blogs, 9 YouTube channels, 6 newsletters and 4 gear comparison sites. Northpeak approved 18 invites; 7 joined on commission and 2 asked for a paid post.

title: Renew the creator deals that pay back
summary: Each month, rank every creator deal by what it brought in for what it cost, draft renewals for the winners and a polite pass for the rest.
description: Once a few creator deals have run, the question is which to do again. This playbook lines up every partnership's spend against the visits, sign-ups and paying customers from its link and code, ranks them, and drafts a renewal for each one that paid back and a kind note to the ones that didn't, so the next month's budget goes where it works.

data.label: Partnerships on the board with their results

connections.label: An AI model, unless you run this from your own AI app

inputs.name: target
inputs.label: Most you'll pay for a customer
inputs.help: Deals that cost less per paying customer than this are renewed.

steps.say: Read the brand's context, and list partnerships at Live or Measured.
For each one, add up its recorded spend and its visits, sign-ups and paying customers from its link and code.
Rank them by cost per paying customer, mark each as renew, renegotiate or stop against the target, and move them to Measured.
Draft a renewal for each one to renew, a new rate for each to renegotiate, and a short thank-you for the rest, held until a person approves them.
Once the person decides, move each partnership to Renewed or Declined.

guardrails: Never agree a renewal, a new rate or a payment without a person's approval.
Keep the numbers you share with a creator to their own deal.

measure.how: Across creator deals, this month against last.
Spend on renewed deals divided by all creator spend.

prompt: Review {{brand}}'s creator partnerships. Rank every deal at Live or Measured by cost per paying customer, renew the ones under {{target}}, suggest a new rate for the close ones and a polite pass for the rest. Draft each message for me to approve.
example: Northpeak had six live deals. Two newsletters cost 38 and 44 USD per paying customer and were renewed, one video at 95 USD got a lower rate offer, and three were thanked and dropped.

kit.summary: A Partnerships pipeline for creator, newsletter and podcast deals, creator fields on people, and email drafts for briefs, go-live reminders and thank-yous.

title: Run creator partnerships from first find to results
summary: Find creators your buyers already follow, pitch them personally, track every deal on a Partnerships board, and see which ones paid off.
description: Creators, newsletters and podcasts reach the people you want, but the work around them is messy: a spreadsheet of names, pitches lost in inboxes, fees nobody adds up, and no idea which post brought sign-ups. This playbook sets up a Partnerships pipeline in the CRM, finds creators who already cover your space, drafts a personal pitch for each one you approve, gives every deal its own tracked link, and reports sign-ups and cost per deal, so you renew what works and drop what doesn't.

data.label: A mailbox to send pitches from

connections.label: An AI model, unless you run this from your own AI app

inputs.name: topics
inputs.label: What your buyers watch and read about
inputs.help: A few topics, so the agent looks for creators in the right places.

inputs.name: budget
inputs.label: Budget per partnership
inputs.help: Leave it empty to start with free product and commission deals only.

steps.say: Read the brand's context, and check its setup kit is applied so the Partnerships board and creator fields are there.
Look at partnerships already on the board, so nobody is pitched twice.

Find creators who already cover the topics, starting with people in your own records who create, then the web through your AI app. Add each one as a person with their platforms, audience size and topics, and a partnership at Found.
Vet each one (recent posts, audience fit, past sponsors) and move them to Vetted or Declined with a one-line reason.
Draft a short, personal pitch for each vetted creator as a sequence, held until a person approves the sends.
Watch for replies and move partnerships to Negotiating or Declined. For each agreed deal, make its own tracked link and promo code, save them on the partnership, and record the fee as spend.
When a post goes live, save its link and move it to Live; after two weeks, report visits, sign-ups and cost per sign-up for each, and move it to Measured.

guardrails: Never send a pitch, accept terms or promise money without a person's approval.
Only use contact details a creator publishes for business, and never contact anyone who opted out.
Ask every creator to label the post as sponsored the way their platform requires.
Stay within the budget per partnership, if one was given.

measure.how: Partnerships at Live or later on the board.
Sign-ups from each partnership's tracked link.
Each partnership's recorded spend divided by its sign-ups.

prompt: Run creator partnerships for {{brand}}. Their buyers follow creators, newsletters and podcasts about {{topics}}. Find ten creators who already cover this, vet them, and draft a personal pitch for the best five. Track every one on the Partnerships board, give each agreed deal its own tracked link, and keep each deal within {{budget}}. Nothing is sent or agreed until I approve it.
example: Northpeak sells trail running gear. The agent found twelve creators, three of them already Northpeak customers, vetted eight, and drafted five pitches. Two agreed: a newsletter for a flat fee and a YouTube channel for free product plus commission. After two weeks the newsletter brought 41 sign-ups at 12 USD each and was renewed.

title: Seed your product to creators
summary: Offer free product or credits to a vetted list of creators, give each a code and link, and follow up when they post.
description: Many creators will try a product for free and talk about it if they like it. Seeding costs little, but it only works if the list is right, the offer is clear and nobody is left without a follow-up. This playbook picks creators who fit, sends a short offer, gives everyone who accepts their own link and code, records what the product cost you, and checks back when they post.

data.label: A mailbox to send offers from

connections.label: Payments, to see which codes turn into paying customers
An AI model, unless you run this from your own AI app

inputs.name: offer
inputs.label: What you give
inputs.example: a free pair of trail shoes

steps.say: Read the brand's context, and check its setup kit is applied so the Partnerships board and creator fields are there.
Pick creators from the board at Found or Vetted who fit the offer, and suggest more from your own records who create, up to the number given.
Draft a short offer that says what they get and that there's no obligation to post, as a sequence held until a person approves it.

For each creator who accepts, set the deal type to free product, make their tracked link, save it and their promo code on the partnership, record what the product cost as spend, and move it to Agreed.
Two weeks later, check who posted, save the post link and move them to Live; suggest a friendly nudge for the rest.
After a month, report visits, sign-ups and paying customers per creator, and say who to offer a paid deal.

guardrails: Never send an offer or ship anything without a person's approval.
Never ask for a positive review or make posting a condition of the gift.
Ask every creator who posts to say they got the product free, the way their platform requires.

measure.how: Creators who posted divided by creators who accepted.
Paying customers from each creator's link and code.

prompt: Seed {{brand}}'s product to {{how_many}} creators. Offer {{offer}}, with no obligation to post. Pick creators who fit from the Partnerships board and our own records, give everyone who accepts their own link and code, and follow up when they post. Nothing is sent until I approve it.
example: Northpeak offered shoes to 20 creators. Fourteen accepted, nine posted within two weeks, and three of them brought more than 10 paying customers each. Those three were offered a paid video.

title: Sponsor newsletters and podcasts that pay back
summary: Shortlist newsletters and podcasts your buyers read, ask for rates, book small test slots, and scale the ones that bring paying customers.
description: Newsletter and podcast sponsorships are easy to buy and hard to judge. This playbook shortlists the ones that reach your buyers, compares them by price per 1,000 readers or listeners, books one small test slot at a time, and gives each slot its own tracked link and promo code, so the next decision is based on paying customers, not opens.

data.label: A mailbox to ask for rates from

connections.label: Web search, unless your AI app searches the web itself
An AI model, unless you run this from your own AI app

inputs.name: topics
inputs.label: What your buyers read and listen to

inputs.name: test_budget
inputs.label: Budget for the first test slots

steps.say: Read the brand's context, and check its setup kit is applied so the Partnerships board is there.
Look at partnerships already on the board, so nobody is asked twice.
Shortlist newsletters and podcasts on the topics, with their audience size and published prices, and work out the price per 1,000 readers or listeners where they share it.
Add each one as a company with its host or editor as a person, and a partnership at Found with the platform, deal type flat fee and the published price as the fee.
Draft a short rate card request to the best shortlisted ones that don't publish prices, as a sequence held until a person approves it.

Suggest which test slots to book within the budget, cheapest per reader first. For each slot a person books, make its tracked link, save it and the promo code on the partnership, and record the fee as spend.
Thirty days after each slot runs, report visits, sign-ups, paying customers and cost per paying customer, and say which to book again.

guardrails: Never book a slot, agree a price or pay anyone; a person does that from their own account.
Stay within the test budget.
Ask every newsletter and podcast to label the slot as sponsored.

measure.how: Each slot's recorded fee divided by paying customers from its link and code.
Partnerships that reach Renewed.

prompt: Find newsletters and podcasts about {{topics}} that {{brand}}'s buyers read and listen to. Shortlist them by price per 1,000 readers, ask the best ones for rates, and suggest test slots within {{test_budget}}. Track each slot on the Partnerships board with its own link and code, and tell me after 30 days which ones to book again. Nothing is booked or sent until I approve it.
example: Northpeak shortlisted 18 newsletters and 6 podcasts. Two test slots were booked for 1,300 USD in all. After 30 days the newsletter brought 9 paying customers at 44 USD each and the podcast 1 at 900 USD, so the newsletter was booked again and the podcast was dropped.

title: Write content from your customers' questions
summary: Turn the questions people ask in replies into briefs for pages that answer them in search.
description: The questions prospects and customers ask by email are the same ones others type into search and AI assistants. This playbook collects them from the inbox, groups the ones that come up again and again, checks whether the site already answers them, and writes a short brief for each page that's missing.

connections.label: An AI model, unless you run this from your own AI app

inputs.name: days
inputs.label: How far back to look, in days

steps.say: Read replies from the period and pull out every question.
Group questions that mean the same thing and count them.
Check which ones the site already answers and which pages target them.
Write a brief for each missing page and post them to the mission.

guardrails: Briefs never quote a customer by name or include their email address or company.

measure.how: Search Console clicks to pages written from the briefs.
How often the same questions arrive by email, before and after.

prompt: Run the "Content from customer questions" playbook. Read the replies from the last {{days}} days and pull out every question people ask about our product or problem. Group the ones that mean the same thing and count them. Check which ones our site already answers, then write a short brief for a page that answers each of the top five that it doesn't. Never quote anyone by name or include their email address or company.
example: Northpeak's inbox asked "can I export to CSV?" 23 times in 90 days and the site had no page about it. The brief became a docs page that now ranks first for "northpeak csv export".
